news.content: My Markets Watchlist Markets News Search Business Strategy Economy Finance Retail Advertising Careers Law Media Real Estate Small Business The Better Work Project Personal Finance Tech Science AI Enterprise Transportation Startups Innovation Markets News Stocks Indices Commodities Crypto Currencies ETFs Lifestyle Entertainment Culture Travel Food Health Education Parenting Military & Defense Politics Reviews Home Kitchen Style Streaming Pets Tech Deals Gifts Tickets Video Big Business So Expensive View From Above Small Business Authorized Account Risky Business Boot Camp Still Standing How Crime Works Life Lessons Level Up Community Games Boxed Pipeline Knighthop Tally Rabies in Cape Fur Seals: What New South African Research Could Mean for Canada PRESS RELEASE GlobeNewswire Sep. 23, 2026, 06:00 AM OTTAWA, Ontario, Sept. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The Canadian Animal Health Institute (CAHI) is proud to continue its annual tradition of hosting an educational webinar in recognition of World Rabies Day. This year’s event will explore the theme, “Stronger Together: Canada’s Evolving Rabies Landscape.” Date: Monday, September 28, 2026 Time: 12:00 p.m. ET Location: Free online webinar (advance registration required) Rabies crosses species, regions and borders, making collaboration among governments, researchers, veterinary professionals, industry and communities essential to effective prevention and control. The webinar will bring together experts to examine two timely developments that demonstrate the evolving nature of rabies risks in Canada and around the world: Rabies in South African Cape fur seals: Dr. Lesley van Helden, State Veterinarian for Western Cape Department of Agriculture will discuss the emergence of a jackal rabies virus strain in Cape fur seals and initial efforts to vaccinate affected seal populations. This topic is highly relevant to the Canadian context, as Arctic fox rabies is endemic in the north and the potential for transmission of the virus exists when rabid foxes come into contact with seals and other marine mammals on sea ice and coastlines. Raccoon rabies in Quebec: Ariane Massé, PhD, a biologist with the Wildlife Health and Welfare Directorate at Québec’s Ministry of the Environment, will provide an update on the ongoing raccoon rabies outbreak in Quebec and the measures being taken to protect animals, people and communities. The webinar will open with special greetings from Member of Parliament Anita Vandenbeld and Coco, the 2026 Cutest Cat on Parliament Hill. “Rabies does not recognize geographic or species boundaries, and neither can our response,” said Dr. Catherine Filejski, President and CEO of the Canadian Animal Health Institute. “By bringing together expertise from Canada and around the world, we can strengthen awareness, support effective prevention and control measures, and better support healthier animals for a healthier Canada.” CAHI’s 2026 World Rabies Day Webinar is made possible through the generous support of Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health Canada and Ceva Animal Health Canada. Registration is complimentary and now open through the CAHI website or the webinar registration page. About the CAHI Established in 1968, CAHI is the trusted, science-based voice of the Canadian animal health industry. Our members provide Canada’s veterinarians and animal owners with the animal medications and tools necessary to maintain the health of our pets and food animal population. Healthier animals for a healthier Canada. www.cahi-icsa.ca. Contact: Eleanor Hawthorn, Communications Manager, ehawthorn@cahi-icsa.ca Markets Insider and Business Insider Editorial Teams were not involved in the creation of this post. news.source_body_en: The Canadian Animal Health Institute (CAHI) is hosting an educational webinar on September 28, 2026, to discuss rabies in Cape Fur Seals and raccoon rabies in Quebec as part of World Rabies Day. The event, titled 'Stronger Together: Canada’s Evolving Rabies Landscape,' will explore the cross-species and cross-border transmission of rabies, emphasizing the need for collaboration among governments, researchers, and communities. Dr. Lesley van Helden will present on the emergence of a jackal rabies virus strain in Cape fur seals and initial vaccination efforts, while Ariane Massé will update on the ongoing raccoon rabies outbreak in Quebec. The webinar aims to strengthen awareness and prevention measures, with a focus on protecting both animals and humans. Registration is open and free, highlighting CAHI's commitment to animal health and public safety.
news.content_zh: 加拿大动物健康研究所(CAHI)将于2026年9月28日举办一场教育性网络研讨会,讨论狂犬病在南非海豹以及魁北克地区的浣熊狂犬病的情况,作为世界狂犬病日的一部分。活动标题为《携手共进:加拿大狂犬病形势的演变》,将探讨狂犬病的跨物种和跨境传播,强调政府、研究人员和社区之间合作的必要性。Lesley van Helden博士将介绍在南非海豹中出现的豺狂犬病病毒株以及初步的疫苗接种努力,而Ariane Massé将更新魁北克地区持续的浣熊狂犬病监测情况。此次网络研讨会旨在增强对狂犬病的认识并加强预防措施,重点保护动物和人类。注册是开放且免费的,突显了CAHI在动物健康和公共安全方面的承诺。

Infectious DiseasesSeptember 21, 2026 CDC rabies warning: Infectious diseases expert explains when a bat encounter requires medical care By Marianne Russ Sharp Watch Video Rabies Explained: Symptoms, Transmission and Treatment Rabies is nearly 100% fatal without intervention, but prompt care can save your life Key takeaways Rabies is spread mostly through animals; most commonly bats in California An exposure means you’ve been bitten, scratched or exposed to the saliva of the animal by touching it. Post-exposure prophylaxis, a series of shots, works well and saves lives. (SACRAMENTO) Rabies is something you probably don’t expect to encounter, but UC Davis Health experts say if you’re exposed, there’s little room for error. A recent advisory about increased rabies exposures nationwide has prompted a lot of questions about rabies exposure and management. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) warning said the use of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, a series of shots, was up significantly over the summer in several states. “The reason that we care so much about rabies is that it’s nearly 100% fatal,” said Dean Blumberg, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UC Davis Health. The good news, Blumberg noted, is that post-exposure prophylaxis is very effective and saves lives. But it’s critical to know what counts as an exposure and when you should seek medical care. What is rabies and how is it spread? Rabies is a viral disease that spreads mainly through bites or scratches from infected animals, most commonly bats in California. In other parts of the country, raccoons, skunks and foxes may also spread the disease. The old stereotype about rabies being spread by dogs is no longer accurate. Thanks to a strong pet vaccination program, the last known case of rabies transmitted by a dog to a human in California was more than 70 years ago, Blumberg said. Rabies in humans is rare. Fewer than 10 deaths are reported each year, according to the CDC. But it is found in wildlife nationwide (except Hawaii) so it’s important to know what to look for. Can you get rabies without being bitten? You can get rabies without being bitten. Scratches or exposure to oral secretions from an infected animal can also lead to infection. It is common in many parts of California to see bats flying around outside, especially at dusk. Blumberg said being outside and seeing them fly overhead does not count as an exposure. “The real concern is if somebody touches a bat or if they pick up a bat,” he explained. “Children are naturally curious and may come across a wounded, injured or dead bat and may pick it up, touch it or examine it. Even touching it would be considered a significant exposure.” Blumberg said that type of exposure poses a risk for infection and medical intervention would be needed. Should I worry about rabies if there is a bat in my house? Bats are the animals most likely to spread rabies in California. The concern with a bat in the house is whether anyone comes into contact with it or touches it. The goal would be to get the bat out of the house without touching it. But if you wake up and find a bat has been in the house while you are sleeping, experts say you may not know whether you’ve been exposed or not, which could be a concern. “The teeth are so small, that if people are asleep, for example, they may not even know that they were bitten by a bat,” Blumberg said. Even with a careful examination, it may not be clear that there was a bite, so if you wake up with a bat in the house, Blumberg said a primary care provider can help you determine next steps. When should I seek medical care after a bat encounter? If there is any chance that you’ve been exposed to secretions, a bite or scratch, or have touched the bat, contact your primary care provider. What should I do after a possible bat exposure? Do not touch the bat. Wash any bite or scratch with soap and water. Contact your primary care provider immediately. Do not wait for symptoms to develop before seeking care. What are the symptoms of rabies? You will want to seek medical care after a possible rabies exposure before any symptoms are present. Don't wait. There are no real symptoms at first, as it can take weeks to months for the rabies virus to travel to the central nervous system — to the brain, where infections can be potentially fatal. If it does infect the brain, then rabies causes encephalitis. People start off with a fever and very non-specific symptoms, but then eventually they become confused. They might become afraid of water, they might have seizures, they might become aggressive and eventually they end up in a coma and pass away. Seeking medical care as soon as you suspect you might be exposed is critical. Learn more about zoonotic diseases What is the care for possible rabies exposure? If you have a known or suspected rabies exposure, you should reach out to your primary care physician right away. They will likely also contact public health authorities to determine if wildlife in the area have tested positive for the virus. Typical care includes cleaning of the wound (if there is one) and a series of shots, including rabies immune globulin and vaccine, called post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP. “If we know somebody has been bitten or scratched or exposed, then we can prevent it from infecting the brain by giving post-exposure prophylaxis,” Blumberg explained. Post-exposure prophylaxis is highly effective. You may remember hearing stories about a long series of painful rabies shots, but Blumberg noted that things have changed. “The vaccine has been improved and there are fewer doses and fewer side effects, so that should not deter someone from getting the injections if they have been exposed,” he said. About 100,000 Americans are treated for possible rabies exposure each year, according to the CDC. The bottom line about rabies Rabies is nearly always fatal without intervention, but post-exposure prophylaxis, a series of shots delivered after exposure, is effective and readily available. If you think you’ve been exposed to rabies through contact with a bat or other animal, contact your primary care provider right away. Infectious DiseasesSeptember 21, 2026 CDC rabies warning: Infectious diseases expert explains when a bat encounter requires medical care By Marianne Russ Sharp Watch Video Rabies Explained: Symptoms, Transmission and Treatment Rabies is nearly 100% fatal without intervention, but prompt care can save your life Key takeaways Rabies is spread mostly through animals; most commonly bats in California An exposure means you’ve been bitten, scratched or exposed to the saliva of the animal by touching it. Post-exposure prophylaxis, a series of shots, works well and saves lives. (SACRAMENTO) Rabies is something you probably don’t expect to encounter, but UC Davis Health experts say if you’re exposed, there’s little room for error. A recent advisory about increased rabies exposures nationwide has prompted a lot of questions about rabies exposure and management. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) warning said the use of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, a series of shots, was up significantly over the summer in several states. “The reason that we care so much about rabies is that it’s nearly 100% fatal,” said Dean Blumberg, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UC Davis Health. The good news, Blumberg noted, is that post-exposure prophylaxis is very effective and saves lives. But it’s critical to know what counts as an exposure and when you should seek medical care. What is rabies and how is it spread? Rabies is a viral disease that spreads mainly through bites or scratches from infected animals, most commonly bats in California. In other parts of the country, raccoons, skunks and foxes may also spread the disease. The old stereotype about rabies being spread by dogs is no longer accurate. Thanks to a strong pet vaccination program, the last known case of rabies transmitted by a dog to a human in California was more than 70 years ago, Blumberg said. Rabies in humans is rare. Fewer than 10 deaths are reported each year, according to the CDC. But it is found in wildlife nationwide (except Hawaii) so it’s important to know what to look for. Can you get rabies without being bitten? You can get rabies without being bitten. Scratches or exposure to oral secretions from an infected animal can also lead to infection. It is common in many parts of California to see bats flying around outside, especially at dusk. Blumberg said being outside and seeing them fly overhead does not count as an exposure. “The real concern is if somebody touches a bat or if they pick up a bat,” he explained. “Children are naturally curious and may come across a wounded, injured or dead bat and may pick it up, touch it or examine it. Even touching it would be considered a significant exposure.” Blumberg said that type of exposure poses a risk for infection and medical intervention would be needed. Should I worry about rabies if there is a bat in my house? Bats are the animals most likely to spread rabies in California. The concern with a bat in the house is whether anyone comes into contact with it or touches it. The goal would be to get the bat out of the house without touching it. But if you wake up and find a bat has been in the house while you are sleeping, experts say you may not know whether you’ve been exposed or not, which could be a concern. “The teeth are so small, that if people are asleep, for example, they may not even know that they were bitten by a bat,” Blumberg said. Even with a careful examination, it may not be clear that there was a bite, so if you wake up with a bat in the house, Blumberg said a primary care provider can help you determine next steps. When should I seek medical care after a bat encounter? If there is any chance that you’ve been exposed to secretions, a bite or scratch, or have touched the bat, contact your primary care provider. What should I do after a possible bat exposure? Do not touch the bat. Wash any bite or scratch with soap and water. Contact your primary care provider immediately. Do not wait for symptoms to develop before seeking care. What are the symptoms of rabies? You will want to seek medical care after a possible rabies exposure before any symptoms are present. Don't wait. There are no real symptoms at first, as it can take weeks to months for the rabies virus to travel to the central nervous system — to the brain, where infections can be potentially fatal. If it does infect the brain, then rabies causes encephalitis. People start off with a fever and very non-specific symptoms, but then eventually they become confused. They might become afraid of water, they might have seizures, they might become aggressive and eventually they end up in a coma and pass away. Seeking medical care as soon as you suspect you might be exposed is critical. Learn more about zoonotic diseases What is the care for possible rabies exposure? If you have a known or suspected rabies exposure, you should reach out to your primary care physician right away. They will likely also contact public health authorities to determine if wildlife in the area have tested positive for the virus. Typical care includes cleaning of the wound (if there is one) and a series of shots, including rabies immune globulin and vaccine, called post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP. “If we know somebody has been bitten or scratched or exposed, then we can prevent it from infecting the brain by giving post-exposure prophylaxis,” Blumberg explained. Post-exposure prophylaxis is highly effective. You may remember hearing stories about a long series of painful rabies shots, but Blumberg noted that things have changed. “The vaccine has been improved and there are fewer doses and fewer side effects, so that should not deter someone from getting the injections if they have been exposed,” he said. About 100,000 Americans are treated for possible rabies exposure each year, according to the CDC. The bottom line about rabies Rabies is nearly always fatal without intervention, but post-exposure prophylaxis, a series of shots delivered after exposure, is effective and readily available. If you think you’ve been exposed to rabies through contact with a bat or other animal, contact your primary care provider right away. By: Lily O'Shea Becker Posted 11:38 PM, Sep 23, 2026 and last updated 4:04 PM, Sep 24, 2026 KANSAS CITY, Mo. — KSHB 41 reporter Lily O’Shea Becker covers Franklin and Douglas counties in Kansas. Share your story idea with Lily. — The Kansas City, Missouri, Health Department is urging awareness and precaution as it has noted an increase in both human exposure to bats and bats testing positive for rabies. Rabid bats are on the rise in Kansas City. Rabies treatment can cost thousands. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE On Sept. 10, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a health advisory saying communities across the country have reported an increase in human exposure to rabid or possibly rabid animals since July. Both the Kansas Department of Health and Environment and KCMO Health Department have issued similar messages, primarily about bats. Chris Morrison/KSHB Dr. Dana Hawkinson, University of Kansas Health System “It is 100% fatal, but getting vaccinated, getting the proper evaluation and treatment will save your life," Dr. Dana Hawkinson, medical director of infection prevention and control for the University of Kansas Health System, said of rabies. Hawkinson said it's important to contact a local health department after a possible exposure to assess the risk of rabies. He also recommends getting an expert to capture and remove bats from living spaces. Rabies transfers from animal to animal via saliva. Saliva can enter a body through a bite or scratch. “It does take time for that rabies virus to travel up your nerves, so that is why we do have time," Hawkinson said. "But it is important to get vaccinated or immunoglobulin after exposure.” Marvia Jones, director of health for the KCMO Health Department, says immunoglobulin injections are only available in emergency rooms. In May, I woke up to a bat flying around my apartment in Kansas City's Midtown neighborhood. “Certainly, waking up in a room and you see a bat, that can be basically an exposure because you just don’t know," Hawkinson said. "Bats are very tiny animals. They have very tiny teeth, very sharp teeth. It is always really hard to know or tell if you have been bitten and exposed to rabies in that way.” Because I woke up to a bat, I visited a local emergency room where I was advised to start the rabies shot series. For the initial round, I was billed $41,589.84 before insurance. During the emergency room visit, I received six shots — the immunoglobulin injection and the rabies vaccine. Lily O'Shea Becker Lily O'Shea Becker's emergency room bill for the first round of the rabies shot series. Experts say bats can squeeze through spaces that are the size of a dime. I suspect a bat entered my room through a crack in my window screen and escaped before it could be captured for testing. Because I was unable to get it tested, I had to follow through with the remaining three rounds of the rabies shot series, including the rabies vaccine. I received the final rabies vaccinations at the infusion clinic of the hospital I initially visited for the first round. Those three rounds would have cost me $16,020.06 without insurance. I was billed $206.25 for the final three rounds and paid $1,731.89 in total for the rabies shot series. Lily O'Shea Becker Lily O'Shea Becker's bill for one of the final three rounds of the rabies shot series. “I just have sort of casually heard people talking about, ‘Man, going to the ER is expensive,’ and we do empathize with that," Jones said. The KCMO Health Department administered 52% more rabies vaccinations in 2026 compared to 2025, according to the department's senior disease investigator, Caylin Henry. While the health department does not provide the immunoglobulin shot required in the first round, it can administer the rabies vaccine for the following three rounds. Chris Morrison/KSHB Marvia Jones, Kansas City, Missouri, Health Department Jones said the health department has resources to help with the cost of those shots. The city's animal control also provides free services to capture the bat for testing "If we can find that the bat was negative for rabies, that saves the person time and money," Jones said. Seven bats have tested positive in Kansas City in 2026. It's the highest number of rabies-positive bats in the city in more than 10 years, according to the health department. Jones said the health department is not trying to scare residents, but is trying to make the public aware of the increase in rabies activity in the city. “We want people to understand there are some steps they can take to prevent exposures in the first place in terms of bats getting into homes and also remind them of the process of what to do when you find a bat," Jones said. news.title_zh: 堪萨斯城出现狂犬病蝙蝠病例激增 - KSHB 41 堪萨斯城
news.source_body_en: The Kansas City, Missouri, Health Department has reported an increase in rabies cases, with 7 bats testing positive in 2026, the highest number in over 10 years. This rise in rabies activity has led to a 52% increase in rabies vaccinations administered compared to 2025. The department is urging residents to take precautions and report bat encounters, as rabies is 100% fatal if untreated. A local resident, Lily O'Shea Becker, shared her experience of being exposed to a bat and receiving a costly rabies shot series, with the initial round billed at $41,589.84 before insurance. The health department provides rabies vaccines for the following rounds but does not administer immunoglobulin shots. They also offer free services to capture and test bats, which can save individuals time and money. Experts emphasize the importance of seeking medical evaluation after potential exposure and recommend capturing bats for testing to avoid unnecessary treatment. The department aims to raise public awareness about the increased rabies activity and the steps to prevent exposure.

news.content: Health & Fitness Rabies Cases Prompt Nationwide Health Advisory: What Long Island Residents Should Know Reports of people exposed to rabid or possibly rabid animals are rising across the country. Here's where Long Island cases stand. LONG ISLAND, NY — Reports of people exposed to rabid or possibly rabid animals are rising across the country, and health officials say it’s important that Long Island residents know what to do after a bite or scratch to prevent a nearly always fatal disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in a Sept. 10 health advisory that it received 17 percent more rabies-related inquiries in July and August compared with the same time last year. At least eight state health departments also reported increased use of preventive treatment, errors in administering it, or both. The agency did not name the eight states. The federal advisory comes amid a continuing resurgence of terrestrial rabies in Suffolk County. As recently as November 2025, cases were largely concentrated in western Suffolk, with rabid animals reported in Amityville, Deer Park, Lindenhurst and Wyandanch. Since then, cases have been confirmed in communities including Melville, Islip, Bay Shore, Babylon, Northport, Kings Park and Smithtown. Find out what's happening in Long Islandfor free with the latest updates from Patch. Suffolk County's most recent case was confirmed Sept. 18, when a raccoon found outside a Smithtown home tested positive for rabies. A pet dog may have been exposed but was current on its rabies vaccination and received a booster, officials said. No human exposures were reported. That animal marked the county's 27th terrestrial rabies case of 2026 and 46th since Feb. 7, 2025. Find out what's happening in Long Islandfor free with the latest updates from Patch. Days earlier, a Babylon resident came into contact with an ill raccoon that later tested positive for rabies. The resident sought medical attention and was reported to be in good health. Another rabid raccoon was found dead on a Bay Shore property during the same period. Those animals became Suffolk County's 43rd and 44th confirmed terrestrial rabies cases since February 2025. A raccoon found at Sunken Meadow State Park in Kings Park also tested positive this month. A park employee found the apparently ill animal Sept. 11 before it died a short time later. No human or pet exposures were reported. Other recent cases have been confirmed in Northport, Islip and Bay Shore, continuing a geographic spread that health officials have been tracking since terrestrial rabies reemerged in the county last year. (Dakota News Now) - As the weather gets cooler, bats will be looking for a warmer place to roost, which could bring them closer to homes and pets. Animal control officials say knowing how to respond could help protect pets from a potentially dangerous encounter. While bat encounters can be concerning, animal control said the numbers show rabies-positive bats are still relatively uncommon. So far this year, Animal Control has responded to 365 bat calls, and 62 of those bats were sent in for rabies testing, said Patty Beckman, Sioux Falls Animal Control supervisor. Only two of those bats have come back positive for the rabies virus. “So not all bats have the rabies virus,” Beckman said. Officials said it can be difficult to tell if a bat is carrying the virus just by looking at it or watching its behavior. “It’s not easy to just look at a bat and its behavior to say, ‘Oh, that’s a rabid bat,’” said Hilary Ward, South Dakota State University assistant professor and veterinary pathologist. That’s why officials say any possible contact should be taken seriously. If a bat scratches, bites, or lands on a person, or comes into contact with a pet, the bat can be sent for testing. “Known contact would be if a bat bites you, if a bat lands on you, if you feel like a bat scratched you—anything like that where a bat would even touch you, and you feel like you had contact, we can definitely send it in for rabies testing,” Beckman said. Pets don’t have to spend time outside to be at risk. “It is very important even for your animals that are strictly indoors to be rabies vaccinated, just in case if a bat would get into your house and they would have contact with that bat,” Beckman said. Ward said rabies is a serious disease and testing can determine whether an exposure occurred. “As a veterinary professional, we are going to err on the side of caution to say, if you’ve had a bat in your home, we recommend that you have that bat tested,” Ward said. Officials say keeping up to date on pet rabies vaccinations is one of the best ways to protect them. If a pet comes into contact with a bat, officials say to reach out to a veterinarian or animal control. Copyright 2026 Dakota News Now. All rights reserved. Boehringer Ingelheim and AWARE launch new Stop Rabies project in Zimbabwe to help protect dogs and communities Boehringer Ingelheim Wed, September 23, 2026 at 4:00 AM EDT 4 min read Boehringer Ingelheim Boehringer headquarters Ingelheim, Germany Rabies remains one of the world's deadliest yet preventable zoonotic diseases, highlighting the need for sustained prevention efforts. Through a new multi-year collaboration, Boehringer Ingelheim and AWARE are expanding dog vaccination, population management and education efforts in rural Zimbabwe. By protecting animal health, the initiative helps safeguard people, communities, and livelihoods. Ingelheim, Germany – As part of its global Stop Rabies program, Boehringer Ingelheim, AWARE Germany e.V. and AWARE Trust Zimbabwe are launching a comprehensive rabies-control initiative in the Tsholotsho District of Zimbabwe, one of the most remote and poorest rural areas in the country. Together, the two veterinary-led AWARE organizations follow a holistic One-Health approach to improve animal welfare, community wellbeing, and wildlife conservation. The collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim combines dog vaccination and population management with education of children to help reduce the burden of rabies in one of the country's most affected regions. Rabies is entirely preventable, yet it continues to claim tens of thousands of lives every year. Rural communities are especially vulnerable, and children are among those most affected. Because more than 99% of human rabies cases originate from infected dogs, vaccinating dogs remains the most effective way to stop the disease at its source and protect both people and animals1. Expanding Stop Rabies in Zimbabwe At the center of the new Stop Rabies project in Zimbabwe is a comprehensive program based at AWARE's veterinary hub in Tsholotsho. Through mobile veterinary teams, the project aims to vaccinate approximately 15,000 dogs every year, reaching an estimated vaccination coverage of more than 90% of the local dog population. The program also includes the free sterilization of at least 1,200 dogs annually, helping support sustainable rabies control and animal welfare. "No one should die from a disease that can be prevented. Through our Stop Rabies program, we are contributing to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies deaths, knowing that this can only be achieved through collective action," says Thaïs Vila, Global Program Lead for Stop Rabies at Boehringer Ingelheim. The collaboration builds on AWARE's longstanding rabies prevention work in Zimbabwe and reflects a shared commitment to protecting interconnected lives. Protecting dogs from rabies is one of the most effective ways to reduce disease transmission, improve human health and strengthen community resilience. Story Continues "We have seen firsthand how sustained vaccination, and community engagement can reduce the burden of rabies. With Boehringer Ingelheim's support, we can expand our reach and strengthen local veterinary services to help protect even more communities across Tsholotsho," says Martin Kessler, Chair of AWARE Germany. Education is another key part of the collaboration. AWARE is expanding its PAWS Clubs (Promoting Animal Welfare Clubs), training 170 teachers across 85 schools and reaching more than 50,000 students with information on rabies prevention, safe interactions with dogs and responsible animal care. Through this collaboration, Boehringer Ingelheim and AWARE are demonstrating how collective action can help protect lives and move communities closer to a future free from dog-mediated rabies. By combining prevention, education and community action, the partnership is helping tackle rabies at its source while building a model that can support long-term progress in affected communities. 1 World Health Organization (WHO). Rabies. https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies About AWARE AWARE Trust Zimbabwe and AWARE Germany e.V. are partner non-governmental organizations dedicated to protecting biodiversity through veterinary outreach, education and wildlife conservation programs. Both organizations are led by veterinarians and work closely with local communities to improve the health and wellbeing of animals, people and ecosystems. Learn more at www.aware-germany.de Boehringer Ingelheim – Animal Health business Boehringer Ingelheim provides innovation for preventing and treating diseases in animals. The company offers a wide range of vaccines, parasite-control products, and medicines for pets, horses, and livestock to veterinarians, animal owners, farmers, and governments. As a leader in animal health, Boehringer Ingelheim values that the health of humans and animals is deeply connected and strives to make a difference for people, animals, and society. Learn more at www.boehringer-ingelheim.com/animal-health. Boehringer Ingelheim Boehringer Ingelheim is a biopharmaceutical company active in both human and animal health. As one of the industry's top investors in research and development, the company focuses on developing innovative therapies that can improve and extend lives in areas of high unmet medical need. Independent since its foundation in 1885, Boehringer takes a long-term perspective, embedding sustainability along the entire value chain. Our approximately 54,300 employees serve over 130 markets to build a healthier and more sustainable tomorrow. Learn more at www.boehringer-ingelheim.com. DOH says don’t delay treatment | Mindanao Gold Star Daily Skip to main content Sunday, September 27, 2026 Cagayan de Oro HOMELATESTNEWSFEATURESABOUTCONTACT US Search Sections OPINIONBUSINESSLIFESTYLE & CULTURESPORTSPHOTOGRAPHYCOMMUNITY DESK Sign in with Google News Animal bite? DOH says don’t delay treatment Ben BalceSeptember 23, 20262 min read Rabies prevention. Dr. John Daniel Estandarte of the Department of Health in Northern Mindanao reminds the public to immediately wash animal bite or scratch wounds with soap and running water before seeking assessment at an accredited Animal Bite Treatment Center. (Photo: PIA-10) CAGAYAN de Oro City — A bite or scratch from an animal should not be treated at home alone, as the Department of Health in Northern Mindanao is reminding the public that quick medical attention can prevent rabies from becoming fatal. Dr. John Daniel Estandarte, medical officer III of the DOH NorthMin Infectious Diseases Cluster, urged people exposed to potentially infected animals to wash the wound immediately and seek treatment at an accredited Animal Bite Treatment Center. “Wash with soap and water, diretso na dayon ka sa mga Animal Bite Treatment Center,” Estandarte said during the Talakayan sa PIA: Konsultayo Series on Sept. 4 at SM CDO Uptown. What to do after a bite DOH advises people with animal bite or scratch wounds to: Wash the wound with soap and running water for 10 to 15 minutes. Go immediately to an Animal Bite Treatment Center for assessment. Follow the recommended post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) treatment schedule. Avoid relying on unverified traditional remedies such as pagtatandok or wound suctioning in place of medical care. Estandarte said dogs account for 95% to 99% of human rabies cases, making prompt assessment important after exposure. He also said bites or scratches involving the head and neck are considered particularly high-risk because the rabies virus attacks the nervous system. Injuries to highly innervated areas such as the hands and face also require prompt medical assessment. “Ang gina-atake sa rabies virus kay ang utok, [anywhere] above the neck, mao na siya ang high risk kaayo,” Estandarte said. Don’t stop treatment early People who have already started PEP but missed a scheduled dose or failed to complete the recommended treatment should return to an accredited Animal Bite Treatment Center, Estandarte said. Health workers can assess the person’s exposure and provide guidance on the next steps. The DOH continues to train health workers and accredit Animal Bite Treatment Centers to improve access to PEP in Northern Mindanao. It also works with the Bureau of Animal Industry and local partners on mass pet vaccination and responsible pet ownership to help prevent rabies transmission. Rabies is preventable through timely post-exposure care, but once symptoms develop, the disease is almost always fatal. (With a report Rushen Mae N. supplementary_news.content_title: FG Begins Free Anti-rabies Vaccination In Gwagwalada, Kubwa - News Agency Of Nigeria
supplementary_news.content: By Felicia Imohimi The Federal Government says it will commence free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs in Gwagwalada, Kubwa and other parts of the country on Saturday, Sept. 26. Dr Samuel Anzaku, Chief Veterinary Officer of Nigeria (CVON) and Director, Veterinary Public Health and Epidemiology, Federal Ministry of Livestock Development (FMLD), said this on Friday in Abuja. Anzaku spoke during a road walk organised to commemorate the 2026 World Rabies Day (WRD), marked annually on Sept. 28. The 2026 commemoration is themed “Stronger Together” The road work was aimed at public enlightenment on rabies prevention, reporting and vaccination. He said the intervention would be implemented by the Federal and state governments in collaboration with development partners, veterinarians and other stakeholders. Anzaku said the vaccination was aimed at reducing the burden of rabies and contributing to the global target of eliminating dog-mediated human rabies by 2030. He urged dog owners to take their pets to designated veterinary clinics for the free vaccination. He also announced plans to provide human pre-exposure prophylaxis to frontline workers who regularly come in contact with dogs. “Veterinarians, paraprofessionals, the hunters who are always in contact with these dogs will be given some pre-exposure prophylaxis against rabies, because you do not have to wait until this problem happens,” he said. Anzaku said the government had lined up activities to translate the World Rabies Day commemoration into concrete actions, especially through mass dog vaccination. “Through the mass vaccination we are targeting two or three area councils beginning from tomorrow,” he said. He described rabies as a preventable viral disease affecting warm-blooded animals, including humans, and said it could be transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, usually following a bite. “In Nigeria, dogs are the principal source of rabies infection in humans,” Anzaku said. He said this year’s WRD theme, “Stronger Together”, underscored the need for collaboration among dog owners, government institutions and other stakeholders. According to him, the One Health approach brings together the Ministries of Health, Environment and Livestock Development, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and other stakeholders. He said the ministry was collaborating with the health and environment ministries, NCDC and World Against Rabies Foundation to raise awareness and strengthen preventive measures. Anzaku also urged the Ministry of Environment to intensify efforts to control stray dogs, describing them as a major contributor to the spread of rabies. He called for active community participation, including traditional rulers, local government chairmen, state governors, development partners and civil society organisations. “It is only through collective effort we will be able to overcome rabies. Prevention is better than cure. Take your dogs to the nearest veterinary clinic. “Report any bite to the nearest hospital so that immediate action can be taken,” he said. Dr George Onyemaowa, National Coordinator, Rabies Control Programme in Nigeria said the road walk was organised to raise awareness about rabies prevention and the need for immediate treatment after a dog bite. Onyemaowa, also the Coordinator, One Health Technical Working Group on Rabies urged members of the public to immediately wash dog-bite wounds with soap and water and proceed to the nearest hospital. Speaking on the prevalence of rabies, he said reports were being received from between 18 and 20 states monthly. “As it stands now, we have over 100 cases already between January and August. And almost every week we keep getting reports,” he said. Onyemaowa identified Plateau, Bauchi and Gombe as among the states reporting high numbers of rabies cases. He listed symptoms in humans to include fever, headache, pain or tingling around the bite, confusion, irritability, fear of water and paralysis, which could result in death. Dr Moses Arokoyo, President, Nigerian Veterinary Medical Association (NVMA), said the association was committed to supporting efforts to eradicate rabies. Arokoyo, represented by Dr Chinnaemeka Joe-Iruobe, Chairperson, FCT chapter of NVMA, said rabies deaths were distressing because the disease was preventable. “I follow the fight against rabies with passion as a veterinarian. If we can eradicate rabies by 2030, I will be the happiest person in the world,” he said. (NAN) FUA/TAK Edited by Tosin Kolade

Health department reminds public of rabies precautions In California, bats are the animal most frequently reported with rabies (Photo courtesy of CA Fish and Wildlife). The Stanislaus County Health Services Agency is hoping to raise awareness about rabies as World Rabies Day approaches. The health caution comes as Stanislaus County has recorded two confirmed cases of rabies in animals, a bat and a skunk, this year. Both of the animals that tested positive for rabies had interactions with domestic pets, reinforcing the importance of vaccinating pets and preventing them from interacting with wildlife, according to the health department. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also recently issued a Health Advisory following increases in reported human exposures to rabid or potentially rabid animals in several areas of the United States. “Rabies is rare, but it is an extremely serious disease that is nearly universally fatal once symptoms develop,” said Thea Papasozomenos, MD, MPH, Stanislaus County Public Health Officer. “The good news is that rabies is preventable. Avoid contact with wild animals, keep your pets vaccinated, and seek medical advice promptly if you think you or a family member may have been exposed.” In 2024, a Dos Palos teacher died after being bitten by a presumably rabid bat in Merced County approximately one month earlier. Deaths from rabies are rare in the United States, with fewer than 10 cases identified each year. Nonetheless, each year, thousands of people receive preventive treatment for rabies following a bite or other direct contact with an animal with possible rabies. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the brain and nervous system. Any mammal, including people and domestic animals, can become infected. In California, bats are the animal most frequently reported with rabies, followed by skunks. Rabies is usually transmitted through the bite of an infected animal but can also spread when infected saliva comes into contact with broken skin or the eyes, nose, or mouth. Once symptoms develop, rabies is nearly always fatal. However, rabies can be prevented when potential exposures are identified and appropriate medical care is received before symptoms develop. Residents should never touch, feed, capture, or attempt to care for wild animals, including those that appear sick or injured. This is especially important with bats because their bites can be small and may not leave an obvious mark. A bat found on the ground or active during the day may be sick or injured and should not be handled. Residents can reduce the risk of rabies by: Keeping pets vaccinated. Make sure pets are current on recommended rabies vaccinations. Avoiding contact with wildlife. Never handle or attempt to care for bats, skunks, or other wild animals. Supervising pets outdoors. Keep pets from approaching or interacting with wildlife. Teaching children to avoid wild or unfamiliar animals, even if an animal appears friendly, sick, or injured. Taking possible exposures seriously. Seek guidance after direct contact with a bat or other potentially rabid animal, even if you do not see an obvious bite. If you are bitten or scratched by a wild or unfamiliar animal, immediately wash the area thoroughly with soap and water and contact a healthcare provider. If you had direct contact with a bat or find a bat in a situation where contact cannot be ruled out, such as in a room with a sleeping person, unattended young child, or someone unable to reliably report whether contact occurred, contact a healthcare provider or Public Health for a rabies risk assessment. When recommended, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is highly effective at preventing rabies when given before symptoms develop. If your pet has contact with a bat, skunk, or other potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian promptly. If a wild animal may have had contact with a person or pet, do not handle or release it before receiving guidance because the animal may need to be tested for rabies. For questions about possible human rabies exposure, contact Public Health at (209) 558-7700. For concerns involving wildlife or domestic animals, contact your local animal control agency. For more information about rabies, visit the California Department of Public Health or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rabies webpages. supplementary_news.content: See photos as Independence celebrates annual Hop & Heritage Festival News Sports Politics Outdoors Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals ENVIRONMENT Bat tests positive for rabies in Albany area. How to stay safe Riley Ellis Salem Statesman Journal Sept. 23, 2026, 1:55 p.m. PT A bat in the Albany area tested positive for rabies on Sept. 22, according to Linn County. An official said the case is part of a wider pattern of bat rabies activity across Oregon this year. As of July, 22 bats had tested positive for rabies in Oregon. People should avoid touching a dead or live bat with bare hands. There is no way to determine if a bat has rabies by appearance. "If you've touched a bat, woken up with a bat in your room, or aren't sure whether you were bitten or scratched, contact a healthcare provider or Linn County Health Services right away," a news release said. "If you are bitten or scratched, wash the area well with soap and water and get medical advice immediately." The rabies virus spreads from infected mammals to humans and is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, officials said. Rabies is preventable if people get medical care before symptoms begin. In Oregon, bats are the only wild species that naturally carries the rabies virus. Foxes, skunks, cats, dogs and other animals can become infected after contact with a rabid bat. Residents are asked to vaccinate dogs against rabies and instruct children to avoid bats and report them to adults. To report an exposure or ask questions, call Linn County Health Services at 541-967-3888 ext. 2488 or 541-750-0090 after business hours. For more information, go to linncountyhealth.org Riley Ellis is an outdoor intern at the Statesman Journal. He can be reached at rellis@statesmanjournal.com. Harford County launches rabies vaccination bait program | Exclusive WBAL US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 2:53 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 7:32 PM EDT Sep 23, 2026 Editorial Standards i Tommie Clark Reporter Harford County health officials deploy vaccination bait program amid rise in rabies cases Number of animals testing positive for rabies in Harford County already matches county's total for all of 2025 Updated: 7:32 PM EDT Sep 23, 2026 Editorial Standards i Tommie Clark Reporter BEL AIR, Md. — Rabies cases are increasing in Harford County, leading health officials to launch a pilot vaccination program to prevent the spread of the disease. | HARFORD COUNTY : Oral Rabies Vaccination Project Advertisement "Harford County is, unfortunately, (where there is) the highest number of rabid animals tested for the state of Maryland, so far," said Hannah Lux, a community hygiene supervisor at the Harford County Health Department. County health officials on Wednesday gave WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates an exclusive look at the vaccination program, which involves strategically placing more than 15,000 vaccine baits across the county. Wild raccoons bite into the bricks or packets and receive immunization. Harford County health officials say they're following the lead of Anne Arundel County's program . So far this year, as many as 28 animals have tested positive for rabies in Harford County, matching the county's total for all of 2025. Raccoons account for 18 of the cases, along with some foxes, groundhogs and bats. On Wednesday, county health officials announced another fox was confirmed to have tested positive for rabies. The fox was found near the 2300 block of Perry Avenue in Edgewood. "We're a little bit higher, but we're also testing a pretty good number of animals. So, the more animals you test, the more likely you are to have positives," Lux told WBAL-TV 11 News. According to data obtained by WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates, Harford County reported 23 rabies cases in 2024, 11 in 2023 and 21 in 2022. "If an animal has had contact with people or pets ... then we would want to test." Raymond, a county resident, shared his experience with rabid raccoons. "I see rabid raccoons all the time. I have one that comes around often enough, he has a name," Raymond told WBAL-TV 11 News. "I always keep my distance." Lux explained that while the numbers are slightly up, they remain in line with expectations as reports of animal exposures have increased nationwide. She emphasized the importance of awareness to help residents respond appropriately to encounters with rabid animals. | MORE : If exposed to rabies, what do you do? "If an animal has had contact with people or pets, like a bite or a scratch, then we would want to test," Lux told WBAL-TV 11 News. Health officials said witnessing a raccoon is not cause for alarm, but if you or your pets have had contact with infected animals, get tested and call the Harford County Health Department at 410-877-2300 for follow-up. Health officials offer the following tips to pet owners: Keep pets leashed when out for walks and closely monitor them while they're in the back yard. All cats, dogs and ferrets should remain up to date on their rabies vaccinations through their vet office or local rabies vaccination clinic. Cover trash cans and do not leave pet food outside. Avoid feeding, petting or interacting with wildlife in any way. Call Harford County Animal Control at 410-638-3505 when you see a stray animal showing abnormal behaviors, such as excessive affection, aggression, lethargy or disorientation. Ashley has told stories all across the country, including in Maine, Central Pennsylvania and Tampa, where she won a Florida Association of Broadcast Journalists award in the "Multi-Media Journalist In a Large Market" category. Read Full Bio Ashley Paul Updated on: September 23, 2026 / 11:18 PM EDT / CBS Baltimore Add CBS News on Google Health officials in Harford County are warning residents after another animal tested positive for rabies Wednesday, pushing the county's total number of cases this year past the number reported in all of 2025. "It's a little spooky, I guess. Definitely unexpected. We play outside all the time, so hearing about rabies is always scary, especially when there's kids involved," said Chris McIntosh of Forest Hill. Neighbors in a Forest Hill community said they are concerned after a rabid groundhog was found in their neighborhood this week. That case was one of four rabies-positive animals reported in the county this week. A rabid groundhog and raccoon were reported from Aberdeen on Tuesday. "Surprising, I mean we've seen some foxes and some other stuff wandering around but having a rabid animal is always concerning," said Christian Taylor of Forest Hill. A fox that tested positive Wednesday marked the 28th rabies case reported in Harford County this year. Why the uptick in rabies cases Ronya Nassar with the Harford County Health Department said the increase could be partly due to greater awareness and more people reporting suspected cases. "Just the awareness in general has really gotten individuals to learn more about rabies. We're really providing the education, and I think that's kind of why we've been seeing more of those cases," Nassar said. Oral Rabies Vaccination Program The latest cases come just weeks after the county announced its Oral Rabies Vaccination Program. So far, officials have distributed more than 1,000 bait packets throughout the county in an effort to vaccinate wild animals that consume them. "We might not see this change overnight with the cases. But we are really hopeful that this program is going to work," Nassar said. Safety reminder for Harford County residents Nassar is reminding residents to make sure their pets are vaccinated and to teach children not to interact with wild animals. Neighbors said they plan to be more cautious after the recent rabies cases. "We always try to keep our distance with animals anyway, let them do their own thing. But yeah, I think I definitely will be more cautious seeing animals, especially if they're behaving strangely," McIntosh said. "We'll definitely look in the backyard a little closer before letting him out at night and make sure we keep an eye on him when he's out there for sure, because that's ugly," Taylor said. Anyone who thinks they may have been exposed to an animal with rabies in Harford County should contact the Harford County Health Department immediately at 410-877-2300. World Rabies Day 2026: Stronger Together against rabies Distributed by EIN Presswire This WRD, communities around the world are coming together under the theme “Stronger Together” to highlight the importance of collaboration to eliminate rabies. Stronger Together reminds us that eliminating rabies takes all of us. By sharing knowledge, coordinating efforts and supporting one another, we can build safer, healthier communities.” — Dr Andre Coetzer, GARC’s Chief Executive Officer. KS, UNITED STATES, September 22, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — This World Rabies Day, communities around the world are coming together under the theme “Stronger Together” to highlight the importance of working together to prevent and eliminate rabies. On 28 September 2026, individuals, communities, governments, healthcare workers, veterinary professionals, educators and organizations will come together to raise awareness about rabies and take action to protect both people and animals. This year’s theme reflects a simple but important truth: rabies elimination is only possible when we work together. Rabies is one of the world’s oldest and deadliest diseases, but it is also entirely preventable. Every year, an estimated 59 000 people die from rabies, with children making up almost half of those deaths. The tools to eliminate dog-mediated rabies already exist: Vaccinating dogs, educating communities, and ensuring that people exposed to rabies know what to do. “Stronger Together reminds us that no individual or organization can eliminate rabies alone,” says Dr Andre Coetzer, GARC’s Chief Executive Officer. “Whether you are a pet owner, a community volunteer, a veterinarian, a healthcare professional, a teacher or a policymaker, everyone has a role to play. When we share knowledge, coordinate our efforts and support one another, we can create safer, healthier communities for people and animals.” Around the world, people are marking World Rabies Day through vaccination campaigns, community outreach, school education programs, public awareness activities, fundraising events and social media campaigns. These efforts demonstrate the power of local action and the importance of partnerships in creating lasting change. GARC, Rabies Alliance initiated World Rabies Day in 2007, and we continue to support communities and organizations working towards rabies elimination. Through the GARC Data Platform, the GARC Education Platform, and the Communities Against Rabies program, we empower communities with the knowledge and skills they need to lead effective rabies elimination efforts. This World Rabies Day, everyone has a role to play. Pet owners can ensure their dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies. Communities can share accurate information and support local vaccination campaigns. Parents and teachers can help children learn how to safely interact with animals and what to do if bitten. Organizations and governments need to work together to strengthen rabies elimination and response systems. GARC believes that collaboration is not optional but essential because every action matters. By working together, we can move closer to a world free from dog-mediated rabies. ENDS About World Rabies Day World Rabies Day is observed annually on 28 September to raise awareness about rabies prevention and highlight global efforts to eliminate the disease. Coordinated by the Global Alliance for Rabies Control, it has been endorsed by international human and veterinary health organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). About GARC, Rabies Alliance GARC, Rabies Alliance is a global non-profit organization committed to ending human and animal deaths from dog-mediated rabies. GARC works with communities, governments, veterinary and public health professionals, educators and other stakeholders to empower communities and support sustainable rabies elimination efforts. For more information about World Rabies Day 2026, visit World Rabies Day.
